case_studies.title: From Assistance to Agency: Rethinking Autonomy and Control in CI/CD Pipelines
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are assuming active roles in Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) workflows, yet the research community lacks a shared vocabulary for describing what it means for CI/CD to be agentic, how much decision authority is delegated, and where control should reside. This paper presents a vision of agentic CI/CD in which the central challenge is not improving task performance but designing authority transfer, defined as the delegation of operational decisions from human-controlled pipelines to agent systems under specified constraints and recourse mechanisms. To structure
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of defining autonomy in Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, the authors built a framework for designing authority transfer from human-controlled pipelines to AI agent systems, and the result is a clearer understanding of how to delegate decision authority in CI/CD workflows. It aims to improve the control and autonomy of CI/CD pipelines by clarifying the role of AI agents. The research focuses on designing authority transfer and recourse mechanisms.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage CI/CD pipelines, here is what to do: review your current pipeline architecture to identify areas where AI agents can assume active roles, assess the decision authority delegated to these agents, and establish clear constraints and recourse mechanisms to ensure control and autonomy. This flags a risk: if your organisation uses AI agents in CI/CD workflows, check your authority transfer protocols immediately to ensure they are well-defined and secure. Consider applying this framework to your CI/CD pipeline design to improve autonomy and control.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper explores a crucial real-world aspect of AI deployment - agent system decision making in CI/CD pipelines. Given its relevance to IT infrastructure and automation, this is an impactful paper with high practical value. IT engineers and consultants can apply this research directly to their work, designing authority transfer and optimizing control in CI/CD pipelines.

case_studies.title: PrefixGuard: From LLM-Agent Traces to Online Failure-Warning Monitors
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now execute long, tool-using tasks where final outcome checks can arrive too late for intervention. Online warning requires lightweight prefix monitors over heterogeneous traces, but hand-authored event schemas are brittle and deployment-time LLM judging is costly. We introduce PrefixGuard, a trace-to-monitor framework with an offline StepView induction step followed by supervised monitor training. StepView induces deterministic typed-step adapters from raw trace samples, and the monitor learns an event abstraction and prefix-risk scorer from terminal outcomes
case_studies.summary: PrefixGuard solves the problem of late intervention in large language model agent tasks by building a framework that creates online failure-warning monitors from agent traces, resulting in a more efficient and effective monitoring system. The researchers built a trace-to-monitor framework with offline and supervised training steps. This helps with early warning systems for tasks that use large language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language model agents, here is what to do: review your current monitoring setup, consider integrating PrefixGuard for early failure warnings, and assess the potential benefits of improved intervention timing. This flags a risk: if your organisation uses large language model agents without robust monitoring, check your failure detection and response processes immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, only relevant to those using large language model agents.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The novelty of PrefixGuard lies in its solution for monitoring LLM-agent execution, which is a common issue in real-world AI deployment. IT engineers working with large language models would find this relevant and value-added. The framework can be used to build or automate warning systems within 90 days, making it suitable for IT engineers and consultants.

case_studies.title: From Specification to Deployment: Empirical Evidence from a W3C VC + DID Trust Infrastructure for Autonomous Agents
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous AI agents now transact at production scale -- 69,000 bots executing 165 million transactions across 50 million USDC in cumulative volume on a single marketplace -- without any shared trust layer between participants. Regulatory frameworks (Singapore IMDA, NIST CAISI, EU AI Act) and major AI laboratories (Anthropic, Google) have independently converged on the same structural requirement: an open, portable, cryptographically verifiable trust infrastructure for autonomous agents that no single vendor can deliver alone. This paper presents MolTrust, a production-deployed implementation
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of trust infrastructure for autonomous AI agents, building a production-deployed implementation called MolTrust, which enables open and portable trust infrastructure. The result is a trust infrastructure that allows autonomous AI agents to transact without a single vendor controlling it. This is relevant to IT work as it involves cloud infrastructure and security.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for autonomous AI agents, here is what to do: review your current trust infrastructure, consider implementing a similar solution to MolTrust, and assess the potential impact on your security and compliance protocols.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel application of trust infrastructure for autonomous agents, with potential real-world impact on IT infrastructure and AI deployment. IT engineers may need to consider the implications of this development on their current systems.

case_studies.title: Towards Apples to Apples for AI Evaluations: From Real-World Use Cases to Evaluation Scenarios
case_studies.abstract: AI measurement science has a wide variety of methodologies and measurements for comparing AI systems, resulting in what often appear to be "apples-to-oranges" comparisons across AI evaluations. To move toward "apples-to-apples" comparisons in real-world AI evaluations, this work advocates for methodological transparency in evaluation scenarios, operational grounding, and human-centered design (HCD) principles. We propose a repeatable process for transforming high-level use cases to detailed scenarios by eliciting use cases from subject matter experts (SMEs) via a structured AI Use Case Workshe
case_studies.summary: This research aims to solve the problem of inconsistent AI system evaluations by creating a standardized process for comparing AI systems. The authors built a repeatable process for transforming high-level use cases to detailed scenarios. The result is a more transparent and consistent method for evaluating AI systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on AI evaluation methodologies rather than cloud infrastructure management. If your organization is involved in AI system development or procurement, this research may be of interest. No immediate action is required for IT infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Papers score relatively high for novelty and IT relevance as it touches upon AI deployment, real-world use cases, and human-centered design in AI. However, value in 90 days is low.

case_studies.title: Beyond the Black Box: Interpretability of Agentic AI Tool Use
case_studies.abstract: AI agents are promising for high-stakes enterprise workflows, but dependable deployment remains limited because tool-use failures are difficult to diagnose and control. Agents may skip required tool calls, invoke tools unnecessarily, or take actions whose consequence becomes visible only after execution. Existing observability methods are mostly external: prompts reveal correlations, evaluations score outputs, and logs arrive only after the model has already acted. In long-horizon settings, these failures are especially costly because an early tool mistake can alter the rest of the trajectory,
case_studies.summary: This research aims to solve the problem of diagnosing and controlling tool-use failures in AI agents, by making AI decision-making more interpretable. The authors built a system to improve the observability of AI tool use. The result is a more dependable deployment of AI agents in high-stakes enterprise workflows.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI-powered workflows, here is what to do: review your existing observability methods, consider implementing more interpretable AI tools, and monitor for tool-use failures to improve overall system reliability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty and relevance from the deployment angle of agentic systems. Value in 90 days comes mainly from the identification of tool-use failures.

case_studies.title: ScarfBench: A Benchmark for Cross-Framework Application Migration in Enterprise Java
case_studies.abstract: Java remains central to enterprise software, and many applications outlive their original architecture. Migrating them across frameworks is a behavior-preserving refactoring spanning build configuration, dependency injection, persistence, request handling, and deployment. Existing software-engineering benchmarks cover bug fixing, feature implementation, and language or version modernization, but leave cross-framework refactoring largely unmeasured. We introduce ScarfBench, a benchmark for behavior-preserving cross-framework refactoring of enterprise Java applications. It is built from expert-w
case_studies.summary: ScarfBench solves the problem of migrating Java applications across different frameworks, the researchers built a benchmark to measure this process, and the result is a tool to help with behavior-preserving refactoring. This benchmark is specifically for enterprise Java applications and aims to fill a gap in existing software-engineering benchmarks. It measures the process of moving applications across frameworks while preserving their original behavior.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage Java-based cloud infrastructure, here is what to consider: check if your organization needs to migrate applications across frameworks, use ScarfBench to measure and optimize this process, and evaluate how it can help with behavior-preserving refactoring. This flags a risk: if your org uses multiple Java frameworks, check your migration processes immediately to ensure they are optimized. If you do not work with Java applications, this research is not directly applicable to your IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novel benchmark for migration, but lacks AI/ML angle. Directly relevant to enterprise software engineering. Provides a specific and actionable assessment of migration process, but implementation would still take time. IT relevance high, but AI maturity is 0 as it does not involve machine learning or automation.

case_studies.title: Empirical Bayes Rebiasing
case_studies.abstract: We study methods for simultaneous analysis of many noisy and biased estimates, each paired with an even noisier estimate of its own bias. The analyst's goal is to construct short calibrated intervals for each parameter. The standard debiasing approach, which subtracts the bias estimate from each biased estimate, inflates variance and yields long intervals. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of reducing variance in biased estimates by introducing an empirical Bayes rebiasing strategy, which constructs short calibrated intervals for each parameter. The authors built a method that learns from data how much bias to reintroduce, resulting in more accurate estimates. This research is not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work.

case_studies.title: Securing Computer-Use Agents: A Unified Architecture-Lifecycle Framework for Deployment-Grounded Reliability
case_studies.abstract: Computer-use agents(CUAs)are moving frombounded benchmarks toward real software environments, wherethey operate browsers, desktops, mobile applications, flesystems,terminals, and tool backends. In such settings, reliability isno longer captured by task success alone: perception errors,planning drift, memory use, tool mediation, permission scope,and runtime oversight jointly determine whether agent actionsremain aligned with user intent, Existing surveys organize theCUA landscape by methods, platforms, benchmarks, or securitythreats, but less explicitly connect capability formation, author-ity
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of securing computer-use agents by creating a unified architecture-lifecycle framework for deployment-grounded reliability, which was built and tested to improve the reliability of agents in real software environments, resulting in more aligned agent actions with user intent. The framework considers multiple factors such as perception errors and permission scope. This framework aims to improve the trustworthiness of computer-use agents in various settings.

case_studies.title: CA-SQL: Complexity-Aware Inference Time Reasoning for Text-to-SQL via Exploration and Compute Budget Allocation
case_studies.abstract: While recent advancements in inference-time learning have improved LLM reasoning on Text-to-SQL tasks, current solutions still struggle to perform well on the most challenging tasks in the Bird-Bench (BIRD) benchmark. This is due to inadequate solution space exploration, which is necessary to uncover promising candidate queries that can be further refined to produce the correct output. To address this challenge, we introduce CA-SQL, a novel Text-to-SQL pipeline that utilizes the estimated difficulty of a task to dynamically scale the breadth of the exploration for generating solution candidate
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient Text-to-SQL task execution by introducing CA-SQL, a pipeline that dynamically scales exploration based on task difficulty. The result is improved performance on challenging tasks in the Bird-Bench benchmark. This research is not directly relevant to managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on natural language processing and Text-to-SQL tasks, rather than cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes an improvement to LLM-based solutions, but it focuses on the inner workings of a Text-to-SQL pipeline without directly discussing tools or systems commonly used by IT engineers. However, the use of LLM in the pipeline is a relevant aspect. This paper's application in real-world scenarios is not clear for the IT engineer or consultant as it is more focused on academics than real-world usage.

case_studies.title: Automated alignment is harder than you think
case_studies.abstract: A leading proposal for aligning artificial superintelligence (ASI) is to use AI agents to automate an increasing fraction of alignment research as capabilities improve. We argue that, even when research agents are not scheming to deliberately sabotage alignment work, this plan could produce compelling but catastrophically misleading safety assessments resulting in the unintentional deployment of misaligned AI. This could happen because alignment research involves many hard-to-supervise fuzzy tasks (tasks without clear evaluation criteria, for which human judgement is systematically flawed). Co
case_studies.summary: This research highlights the challenge of automating alignment in artificial superintelligence, where AI agents may produce misleading safety assessments, leading to the unintentional deployment of misaligned AI. The authors argue that alignment research involves hard-to-supervise tasks that are prone to errors. This study focuses on the safety of AI systems and its potential risks, rather than directly impacting cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the safety and alignment of artificial intelligence systems, rather than cloud infrastructure management or IT operations.
